This is just a terrible mish-mash of poorly understood history, omissions and inventions.

A few examples.

"get technical about who was there first"

An ancient historic title carries no weight in international law.

"In about 1250 BCE, the Jewish people went to what was then called Canaan"

The people in 1250 BCE were Israelites, so calling them "Jewish people" is anachronistic.
According to the Book of Joshua the Israelites conquered the land from the people living there, so it was not their land originally.

"the word “Israel” is mentioned in the Quran about 43 times"

The Quran's references to "Israel" are mostly Bani Isra'il, meaning the Children of Israel as a people, not a territory.

"There could never be another Holocaust"

Irrelevant to the Palestinians.

"Each could have their own State, completely autonomous.  Pretty good deal, wouldn’t you think?"

Neither offer was a "pretty good deal".

In 1937 Peel proposed partitioning a country in which Arabs were the large majority, leaving a substantial Arab population inside the Jewish state, and transferring roughly 225,000 Arabs from it, compulsorily if necessary, while the Arab portion would have been joined to Transjordan rather than becoming an independent state. Peel's proposed Jewish state contained much of Palestine's most fertile and economically developed land, including the coastal plain and Jezreel Valley.

The 1947 UN partition plan gave 56% of Mandatory Palestine to a Jewish population that was ~33% of inhabitants and owned roughly 7% of the land, so the Arab rejection wasn't irrational, although maybe not wise in hindsight.

"Nakba for catastrophe. Because they lost. The Arab world says it’s because Arabs were displaced.  But they chose to be displaced."

That is largely untrue. Most fled or were expelled amid fighting, and around 250-300K had left before the Arab armies invaded. Israel then barred their return.

"[1960s] started to refer to themselves as Palestinians"

"Palestinian" identity did not begin in the 1960s. The newspaper Filastin dates from 1911, and the Mandate was named Palestine.

"A Palestinian state has been offered."

A fully sovereign state has never been offered by Israel to the Palestinians. Both Begin and Netanyahu explicitly stated they opposed it.

"Jews have 0.1% of the land that Muslims have."

Muslims are not a monolithic body.

"And according to the Radicalized Muslims, that’s too much."

A tiny minority do not represent the population.

Jitiya Vrat (Jivitputrika Vrat) – Vidhi & Rituals

Jitiya Vrat, also known as Jivitputrika Vrat, is traditionally observed by mothers for the long life, good health, safety and prosperity of their children. It is especially popular in Bihar, Jharkhand and eastern Uttar Pradesh.

🌺 Main Rituals

1. Preparation / Nahay-Khay

On the day before the fast, take a bath and wear clean clothes.
Clean the house and prepare the puja items.
Traditionally, a special meal is taken before beginning the fast.

2. Sankalp (Taking the Vow)

Take a bath early in the morning and wear clean clothes.
Light a diya and worship Lord Surya (Sun God) and Jivitputrika Mata.
Take a sankalp for the long life, good health and well-being of your children.
Traditionally, Jitiya is observed as a Nirjala fast, meaning neither food nor water is consumed during the fast.

3. Puja Samagri
Commonly used items include:

Kusha/Darbha grass and Durva
Flowers
Roli/Kumkum and Akshat (rice)
Incense and diya
Fruits
Prasad/Naivedya
Red or yellow cloth
Jitiya/Jivitputrika representation, according to family tradition

4. Jitiya Vrat Katha
The Jivitputrika Vrat Katha is read or listened to during the puja. Listening to the vrat katha is considered an important part of the observance.

5. Worship of Surya Dev
Surya Dev is given special importance during Jitiya Vrat. Devotees offer Arghya to the Sun God and pray for the protection, health and longevity of their children.

6. Paran (Breaking the Fast)

On the following day, the fast is broken at the prescribed Paran time.
After bathing and completing the morning rituals, bhog/prasad is first offered to the deity.
Water and food are then taken to conclude the fast.
Prayers are offered for the family’s and children’s continued well-being.

text:
According to Grok: Educate yourself
The Trump administration (second term, starting January 20, 2025) reports a combined total of roughly 2.5–3+ million people who have left the U.S. through formal deportations plus self-deportations as of spring 2026, with enforcement continuing into fall 2026. Independent counts of formal removals are in a similar broad range for later periods, but the large self-deportation estimates are heavily disputed.  **Administration figures (DHS / White House):** - Formal deportations/removals: more than 605,000 by late 2025, over 675,000 by January 2026 (one-year mark), and nearly 900,000 by mid-May 2026. - Self-deportations: estimated at 1.6–1.9 million by late 2025 and about 2.2 million by early/mid-2026. - Combined total who left: over 2.5 million by late 2025 / early 2026, and more than 3 million by May 2026 (including the self-deportation estimate).  These appear in DHS statements, White House summaries, and reporting based on them (e.g., claims of negative net migration in 2025). The self-deportation totals largely rest on declines in survey-based estimates of the unauthorized population (such as Current Population Survey data), plus the message that enforcement pressure and incentives are driving exits. The government-assisted program (CBP Home / Project Homecoming, which offers flights and exit stipends of $1,000–$3,000) accounts for a much smaller share—on the order of 70,000 by March 2026 and about 132,000 by mid-July 2026, with more enrolled.  **Independent and more narrowly verified figures:** - Formal removals are lower in early independent tallies but rise over time. TRAC (Syracuse) and the Deportation Data Project (using FOIA data) put ICE-linked or interior deportations in the roughly 230,000–350,000 range through much of 2025, with interior deportations after ICE arrest up about 4–5× versus late 2024. ICE fiscal-year removals were around 320,000 in FY2025 (which overlaps the end of the prior administration) and were running at 350,000+ through mid-2026 in FY2026, on pace for roughly 400,000–460,000 for the full fiscal year. Later administration statements of ~900,000 total deportations by May 2026 are higher and include broader CBP activity; detailed public audited totals reconciling all categories remain limited. - Documented voluntary departures (immigration-judge orders plus the incentive program) are in the tens to low hundreds of thousands—not millions. Judge-granted voluntary departures rose sharply (tens of thousands in FY2025; over 80,000 from January 2025 into early 2026 in one analysis). Analysts at places such as the Center for Migration Studies, Brookings, and Cato have called the multi-million self-deportation claims overstated or methodologically flawed (survey artifacts, inclusion of legal immigrants or other population changes), with more cautious estimates of enforcement-driven voluntary exits often in the low-to-mid hundreds of thousands.  **Ballpark summary for the second term so far (~20–21 months):** Administration total of people who left is about 2.5–3+ million. A more conservative reading grounded in removal statistics plus verified voluntary exits is roughly 0.8–1.5 million, with the gap driven almost entirely by how “self-deportation” is estimated. Interior enforcement and detention have increased substantially relative to the prior baseline, even if annual formal removals have not reached the stated 1-million-per-year target.

text:
What could DEED actually cost Saskatoon?
The numbers below are my own projections and not represent the City of Sasktoon or any other Councillor's position. They're based on how the federal programs that would fund DEED work, which matters because the Province's offer depends entirely on what Ottawa agrees to fund.
The official estimate for the Downtown Event and Entertainment District is still $1.22 billion, in 2024 dollars. Council has asked for an updated figure, and some media reporting already puts it near $1.6 billion, but even at the lower number, here's what the City's share potentially looks like.
We know City Hall's plan presumes a three-way split, so roughly $400M each from Ottawa, the Province, and the remainder from the City. The Province has already agreed and informed Ottawa that they would match federal dollars up to a third of eligible costs.
So what are eligible costs? Federal infrastructure programs have long refused to fund facilities that house professional or semi-professional teams. For Saskatoon, this includes the Blades and the Rush. The arena accounts for $632M of the $1.22B, so if Ottawa sets it aside and funds a third of everything else (the convention centre, theatre, infrastructure, parkade and land), its share comes to about $200M. The Province would then match that, bringing the total to roughly $400M.
That leaves Saskatoon with about $800M to cover, which is twice what the funding plan was built to address.
The City is also negotiating a possible partnership with Muskeg Lake Cree Nation. These discussions are still very preliminary, but that could mean an operating role in the new venues, urban reserve status for the land, and access to federal funding streams the City can't tap on its own.
To be clear, I'm only considering a hypothetical scenario, so let's say a partnership offer covers about half of the City's $800M, which still leaves roughly $400M for Saskatoon to find.
That sounds like we're back to the original plan, but it isn't. Since Council turned down OVG360, the plan has the new combined board for SaskTel Centre and TCU Place operating the district, with the arena's operating revenue helping pay down construction. A partner putting in hundreds of millions would reasonably expect a share of that revenue in return. So the City's remaining $400M might have to be paid with less money coming back in to cover it.
And what about the ticket surcharge, hotel levy and TIF in the current plan were designed for a $400M share under the original assumptions? It should be noted that the hotel levy requires the Province to amend The Cities Act, and that hasn't happened. As well, the TIF and its returns are back-loaded, so we won't see the full impact until years down the road.
As we consider this, what happens if the cost moves toward $1.6B as reported in the media? The same math leaves the City's portion around $540M with a partner covering half its share. Without a partner, the City's portion is just over $1B.
Again, we are waiting for several reports to come back to Council regarding updated costs, projections, SaskTel Centre upgrade costs, etc., and I want to be clear that none of this is a case for or against a partnership. To my understanding, we are still far from any deal coming to Council, and any agreement would also need to go through Muskeg Lake Cree Nation's own approval process. I'm looking forward to the discussions at Council if and when a deal is proposed.
Right now, what we don't know far exceeds what we do know. With so much work going into showing we can afford this, it feels a bit like a teenager saving for a first car: a few more lawns mowed, a few more shifts at my part-time job, and it'll be mine. Before anyone signs for the car, we need to know the real sticker price, and whether we can pay it without breaking Council's commitment of no property tax increases.

Two of the best middleweights of their era, Jose Basora and Holman Williams (left), battle to a 10-round draw at Convention Hall in Philadelphia on october 3, 1944.

On e of the shames of the current generation of boxing fans is that these two names don't even ring a bell for them as they proclaim this weekend's latest winner "The GOAT."

Honestly, sometimes, their ignorance of their own beloved sport's history is astounding and it saddens me.
----------------------------------------------------------
Legendary trainer Eddie Futch would cite Williams and the great Charley Burley as the two finest fighters he ever had the privilege to see and was quoted as saying that he would rather "watch Williams shadow box than watch most other fighters in action."

Williams was known as a boxer-puncher early in his career, but he become a defensive specialist after his hands were broken several times. He had an excellent jab, deft footwork, and a taut defence.
 "Holman Williams was a great boxer, but he never got the recognition because he wasn't a puncher," Futch said. "He had the finesse of a Ray Robinson, but no punch."
Williams scored victories over notable boxers such as Steve Belloise, Eddie Booker, Charley Burley, Cocoa Kid, Lloyd Marshall, Archie Moore, Bob Satterfield, and Kid Tunero.

From Feared Fighters: Boxing's Black Murderers Row:

Feared, avoided and too good for their own good. Across the 1930s to 1950s, a group of eight fighters became known as ‘Black Murderers Row’.
Talented black contenders who were heavily ducked by the top champions of their era, they were forced to face each other in over 60 total gruelling fights. 
Despite their reputation and ability, none of these renowned fighters were ever given their deserved opportunity to contest for a world title in their otherwise illustrious careers. 
Those denied contenders were Charley Burley, Holman Williams, Cocoa Kid, Lloyd Marshall, Eddie Booker, Jack Chase, Bert Lytell and Aaron Wade. 

We'll stick to WIlliams for now so back to the above article:

Iconic boxing trainer, Eddie Futch, once stated that he’d prefer to watch Holman Williams spar than see most fighters compete in the ring. 
Competing across three different divisions in his illustrious career, Williams honed his renowned technical and defensive skills in the same Detroit gym as the great heavyweight champion Joe Louis. 
Denied a title shot in any of the weights he starred in, Williams was hugely respected during his time and became a very popular contender among fans, who always travelled to witness his talents from ringside.
Despite a career of nearly 190 professional clashes, the Florida-native sadly never fought for a world title. 
But he was involved in many epic encounters with fellow members of Murderers Row and, while most rank Burley as the top of those eight avoided names, many argue Williams was the most outstanding boxer of the group.
----------------------------------------------------------
When talk comes to the great Puerto Rican boxers of all-time the name of Jose Basora should be on everyone's list.

The Forgotten Jose Basora Story By Carlos Acevedo for IBRO:

Jose Basora, one of the toughest, sharpest dressed middleweights of the 1940s, owed his extraordinary career to a dynamic bantamweight named Sixto Escobar. Along with other Puerto Rican pioneers such as Angel Cliville, Atilio Sabatino, and Pedro Montanez, Escobar, at only 5’4”, put Puerto Rico on the boxing map with fists as hard as coconuts. Little Escobar became the first Boricua to win a world title when he knocked out Baby Casanova in 1934. What is truly amazing, however, is that Escobar accomplished this feat only seven years after boxing had been legalized in Puerto Rico. Needless to say, “El Gallito” became an idol from Fajardo to San German.
One of thousands of campesinos inspired by the oversized heroics of the undersized Escobar was Jose M. Basora from Lajas. Basora, born on February 8, 1918, took up boxing as a teenager in Cabo Rojo and went on to become lightweight amateur champion of Puerto Rico. In 1938, Basora won the Gold Medal at the Pan-American Games (then known as the Central American and Caribbean Games) in Panama City and sailed, without a lick of English, for the bright lights of New York where the “Tropical Style” flourished in the late 1930s.
Basora settled in the Bronx and began his pro career under the joint tutelage of sage Whitey Bimstein and Lou Brix. His manager was a prickly Cuban expatriate and nightclub owner named Angel Lopez. Years later, Lopez would become famous for his tempestuous relationship with Kid Gavilan and infamous for being outed as an undercover front for Frankie Carbo.
Jose Basora, often billed as “Joe,” perhaps to downplay his Latin roots, made his pro debut on January 7, 1939 at the Ridgewood Grove Arena in Queens. Over the next seven years he would become a feared contender whose name–Joe or Jose, take your pick–set off warning signals in anybody who weighed over 135 pounds. He peaked at #4 in The Ring annual ratings in both 1943 and 1944. Basora also drew a solid following along the east coast with his high-pressure style and deadly right cross. “He hits harder with either hand than any man in the ring today,” Lou Brix told sportswriter Jack Cuddy. “When he hits them right they remain unconscious for half an hour or more. And he throws those punches absolutely straight—no swings or telegraphs.”
Basora went undefeated in his first 29 bouts before being overmatched against veteran contender Kid Tunero in Havana in 1941. Tunero, with over 100 fights at the time, had already fought twice for the middleweight title and had beaten, among others, Marcel Thil, Anton Christiforidis, and Ken Overlin. As late as 1942 Tunero was ranked in the top five among middleweights. He pounded out a decision over Basora, and the lanky Puerto Rican subsequently hit a rough patch, losing five of his next seven fights. During that stretch Basora lost two decisions each to veteran middleweight Coley Welch and 2008 Hall of Fame inductee Holman Williams. Welch and Williams were both rated in the top five among middleweights at the time. Add to that list rough and tumble top ten contender Antonio Fernandez, and you almost begin to feel sorry for poor Joe.
It soon became clear that Basora would have to duke it out with mismanagement as well as some of the best fighters of his era. Angel Lopez, as courageous as any manager in the history of boxing, once said, “I don’t care with whom they match my boy, so long as it is the same weight division. I’ve a young welterweight now, Jose Basora. He’s fought 77 fights, won 50 of them by knockouts and 27 by decision. When a matchmaker asks me to sign Basora for a fight, I say ‘o.k.” I don’t even ask whom he wants Basora to fight.” Lopez proved himself to be a man of his word. In four and a half years—from March 1941 to August 1945—Basora faced Jake LaMotta four times, Holman Williams five times, and Coley Welch twice. During that span he also fought Sugar Ray Robinson, Ezzard Charles, Fritzie Zivic, Kid Tunero, and Antonio Fernandez. By then, Chris Dundee was also on board as co-manager, but the avalanche of tough fights never stopped.
In between rumbling with hard case after hard case in the ring, Basora was out cutting a natty figure in swanky nightclubs and dance floors across the city. Still a few years ahead of the post-war Puerto Rican migration boom that would earn New York City the tongue-in-cheek nickname “The Big Mango,” Basora enjoyed the Cuban rhumba/charanga craze along with the Latin fusion of nascent Spanish Harlem, with its mix of Puerto Rican, Mexican, and Central American traditions. “I would rather dance than eat,” Basora said, “which I do both at the Havana-Madrid. It is much more pleasure to dance than to skip rope.” The Havana-Madrid, a Broadway hotspot owned by Angel Lopez, was where Basora did his extracurricular roadwork. Chris Dundee elaborated on this uncommon training technique to syndicated columnist Jack Cuddy: “Basora is the outstanding middleweight in the world today because of his legs,” he explained. “Where does he get those legs? He gets them by dancing the rhumba and conga every night he’s in New York at the Havana-Madrid.”
Basora may have been making his mark in the nightclubs, but in the ring he made his first real mark in 1942 with two furious bouts against Jake LaMotta. “The Bronx Bull” was undefeated in New York City when he faced Basora at the Bronx Coliseum just outside Starlight Park on May 12, 1942. After 10 spectacular rounds the bout was called a draw. It was a grueling fight. “The pair locked heads for the full three minutes in every round,” wrote Meyer Ackerman of The Ring, “and blasted one another dizzy as the crowd roared their approval.” A rematch in June was no less brutal and ended with Basora winning a decision before 7,500 spectators. “It was a savage fight all the way,” remarked Ackerman. But not nearly as savage as what would happen to Basora a few months later against Ezzard Charles in Millvale, Pennsylvania. Charles, the future all-time great, demolished Basora, dropping him six times before finally stretching him out for the count in the fifth round. It was a strange case of matchmaking, to say the least, but with most world titles frozen for the duration of World War II and big money fights as scarce as opponents willing to meet him, Basora accepted whatever came his way, even if that meant ducking through the ropes against budding light heavyweights.
In a remarkable show of durability and cojones, Basora was back in the ring a few weeks after the Charles disaster to kick-start an impressive 22-2-2-1 streak. His only losses during that time were decisions to Jake LaMotta in Detroit and Holman Williams in San Francisco.
Then, on May 14, 1945, Basora fought to a 10-round draw with the greatest prizefighter to ever walk the earth. Sugar Ray Robinson, a 7 to 1 favorite, entered the ring with only a loss to Jake LaMotta tarnishing his 54-1 record. Basora and Robinson met at Convention Hall in Philadelphia in front of over 14,600 spectators. Robinson built up an early lead against Basora with his flashy combinations, but began to wilt from a body attack that had him sagging in the fifth round. Basora pressured Robinson throughout the fight, used head movement and feints to avoid blows, and surprised the crowd with his boxing skills. The fight was up for grabs going into the final round. “A spirited 10th round rally by Robinson failed to pull the bout out of the fire,” reported the newswires. “He caught Basora with sharp lefts and rights and gained the round which save him from a defeat.” An unpopular draw was announced.
“Basora is a tough boy,” said Robinson after the bout. “Maybe not so tough as Jake LaMotta, but tough enough.” Maybe Basora was a little tougher than Sugar Ray let on. It took years for a rematch to take place between the two, and by that time Basora was already on the downside. Years of tough fights caught up with Basora; the punishment he received at the hands of Jake LaMotta during their fourth fight in 1945 and against Tommy Yarosz in 1947 particularly seemed to take a lot out of him. LaMotta, now at his destructive peak, pummeled Basora over nine one-sided rounds before the Puerto Rican sank to the canvas, limp.
There would be no quick return to the ring this time for Basora. He was out of action for five months before picking up the gloves again. Tommy Yarosz was known as a light puncher, but Basora collapsed in the ring after losing a close decision in Detroit and was taken to the hospital with a possible skull fracture.
Although doctors advised him to quit, Basora returned to the ring after a few months of rest. From that point on, Basora, who still had enough to beat a faded Holman Williams twice, was in and out, and never defeated another top-flight fighter again. He lost close decisions to tough Bert Lytell and Bee Bee Wright, fought only four times in 1949, and, when he returned to the ring in May 1950 after a layoff of 9 months, lost a decision to Jimmy Beau.
Naturally, as soon as the Puerto Rican bruiser was at the end of the line, 11 years after his pro debut and 12 years after earning a gold medal at the 1938 Central American Games, he got a “title shot” and a second chance against Sugar Ray Robinson. Billed for the “Pennsylvania State World Middleweight Title,” the rematch took place five years after their initial draw. 
By then the fierce slugger who had whipped Jake LaMotta and Holman Williams was little more than a whisper of himself. A decade of tough fights left Basora in no condition to defeat Robinson.
Basora might as well have entered an abattoir on August 25, 1950 instead of the Scranton Stadium in Pennsylvania. Within seconds of the opening bell, a prime Sugar Ray dropped Basora with a slashing left hook. Basora, with his eardrum now punctured, wobbled to his feet. Three more knockdowns later and the slaughter was over. Basora, along with his career, was counted out after 52 seconds. A cynical crowd booed and cat called until they realized that Basora was not about to get up. The Associated Press reported: “Basora was badly hurt. Dr. Leonard Freda of the State Athletic Commission worked over him for six or seven minutes before he was permitted to leave the ring.”
Before that awful night in Pennsylvania, Basora was a top-ranked middleweight for most of the decade, and a feared puncher who put the hurt on several contenders and, for good measure, a couple of Hall of Famers as well. In addition to defeating LaMotta, Basora took care of former welterweight champion Fritzie Zivic, Henry Chmielewski (who was good enough to beat, Lou Brouillard, Georgie Abrams, and Coley Welch), and kamikaze Philadelphia legend Young Gene Buffalo. Still, the big time seemed to elude him.
The truth of the matter is that Basora, a hard punching pressure fighter with a long jab, was ducked by some of the best boxers of his era. (An exception, of course, is Jake LaMotta, whose grim willingness to fight nearly anyone at any time bordered on pathological.) Dozens of legends have been spun around the often specious claim of being “ducked,” but in this case, some “proof,” albeit circumstantial, actually exists. Natural matchups with the likes of Rocky Graziano, Steve Belloise, and Ernie Vigh never materialized, and one contender, The Cocoa Kid, flat out refused to appear for his match with Basora. In addition, Sugar Ray Robinson pulled out of three scheduled matches with Basora before their first fight, and waited five more years to offer him a rematch despite the fact that nearly 15,000 fans attended their first match in Philadelphia. (Incredibly, Sugar Ray even delayed the second fight in 1950. He was fined $1,000 by the Pennsylvania State Athletic Commission for his vanishing act.) A rematch in Madison Square Garden would have been a natural. Imagine the angles: two New Yorkers headlining, one, Basora, with a dedicated Puerto Rican following; the other, streaking Sugar Ray Robinson, facing only the second man he was unable to subdue in 56 fights.
But it never happened. Why? Good question. From 1945 to 1950 Sugar Ray Robinson fought rematches with the following opponents: Kid Gavilan, Ossie Harris, Don Lee, Cecil Hudson, Freddie Flores, Freddie Wilson, Jake LaMotta, Tommy Bell, Bill Lee, and Henry Brimm. Somehow, oddly, Basora managed to slip through this motley dragnet. Unlike Charley Burley, who was too good but perhaps too dull to risk fighting, Basora was one of several all but forgotten drawing cards of the 1940s. His scheduled bout with mysterious welterweight contender Louis “Cocoa Kid” Hardwick, for example, drew nearly 17,000 fans in Philadelphia. Unfortunately, the Kid never bothered to show up, and Basora knocked out late substitute Al Franklin instead. That was just the kind of luck, it seemed, Basora could count on.
After his drubbing at the hands of Robinson, Jose Basora finished his career on the skids, losing five out of his last six bouts, before retiring with a record of 78-20-7 (44). His record against Hall of Fame fighters is 5-7-3.
In retirement, Basora lived in the Bronx and owned a bodega in the Huntspoint section.
His death, in 1993 in New York City, went largely unnoticed, but a baseball stadium in Lajas, Puerto Rico, bears his name as a testament to the unjustly forgotten accomplishments of one of the greatest Puerto Rican fighters of all time.

‼️INHUMANE‼️ Volusia County deputies booked an Oak Hill man on charges of felony animal cruelty after Animal Services found his starving Catahoula mix off Halbrook Road.
⠀
Johnathan Meyers, 31, is charged with felony aggravated animal cruelty. Detectives say Tanner weighed just over 33 pounds against an ideal near 60. A forensic vet scored him 1 out of 9, the bottom of the scale. Open sores, dehydration, untreated infections. The neglected dog hadn’t seen a vet in four years, according to authorities.
⠀
The call started as a stray pickup. What they found was a dog that was practically skin and bones.

Meyers walked up and said he planned to surrender the dog “next week.” He later told investigators he knew Tanner was suffering and “should have known better,” the affidavit states. Animal Services had already offered him education and resources in September 2025. He apparently declined at the time and continued to let the dog starve.

Director Angela Miedema said, “No dog should ever have to reach the state Tanner was in when he came to us.” She added that Tanner still wants people close. Shelter staff put him on emergency care. He has gained more than 15 pounds and improved from multiple infections. Adoption comes when he is ready.
⠀
On Tuesday detectives moved in to make an arrest.

Meyers backed up asking “Why?” then braced and pulled his hands up acting confused. That move also landed the alleged animal ab*ser a charge of resisting without violence.

A glass pipe found in his pocket field-tested positive for methamphetamine, so he scored himself another charge of possession of drug paraphernalia. He has denied the alleged neglect of the animal.  Bond was set at $3,500 and he has since made bail and is back on the streets.

I haven't verified the below information to be a 100% true but this is more along the lines of what I was thinking when I think of unions having a stronghold on longshoreman hiring practices.  

Private companies already run most US container terminals. What has almost never stuck is using non-union labor to load and unload the ships. When operators or port authorities have tried, the longshore unions have usually stopped them through master contracts, lawsuits, and carrier pressure rather than through a formal ban on private ownership.
How the system actually works
Most large US ports are owned by public port authorities. The terminals themselves are often leased to private operators — SSA Marine (Carrix, controlled by Blackstone), APM Terminals, Maher (Macquarie), and others. Those operators do not freely hire whoever they want for container work.
On the East and Gulf coasts, the International Longshoremen’s Association (ILA) has a master contract with the United States Maritime Alliance (USMX), which represents carriers and terminal operators. On the West Coast, the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) has the equivalent with the Pacific Maritime Association. Those contracts generally require that container handling for covered ships be done by union labor. A carrier that docks at a non-union terminal can be sued for breach and faces the risk of trouble at every other union port it uses.
The main recent attempt: Charleston’s Leatherman Terminal
The clearest modern test was the Hugh K. Leatherman Terminal in Charleston, a roughly $1 billion facility that opened in 2021.
South Carolina, Georgia, and North Carolina had used a “hybrid” model for about 50 years at Charleston, Savannah, and Wilmington. Non-union state employees ran the ship-to-shore cranes and heavy lift gear. ILA members, employed by private stevedores, did the rest of the longshore work (lashing, unlashing, and related deck work). South Carolina tried to open Leatherman on that same hybrid basis.
The ILA sued, arguing that a 2012–13 master-contract clause required new terminals in those states to use bargaining-unit labor for the lift work. USMX carriers stopped calling at Leatherman to avoid contract damages. The National Labor Relations Board and, in July 2023, the Fourth Circuit held that the ILA’s lawsuit was not an illegal secondary boycott. The Supreme Court declined review in February 2024.
The terminal sat largely idle for about three years. In June 2024 the South Carolina Ports Authority and the ILA settled. ILA members gained the right to operate cranes; state employees could join the union or stay with the authority. The old strict split of duties ended at Charleston. Savannah is now the last major port still running cranes with state employees, and the ILA has said it will contest that model at any new Georgia terminal.
Earlier privatization and non-union efforts
Full privatization of port operations has been proposed and mostly rejected, but those fights were about who runs the terminal, not about escaping the union.
Virginia received takeover bids in 2009 from CenterPoint, Carlyle, and Carrix/Goldman Sachs. All were rejected. In 2012 APM Terminals offered a 48-year concession valued at roughly $3–4 billion to operate the state terminals. Competing carriers objected, and the state did not hand over operating control. Virginia International Terminals still runs the facilities and bargains with the ILA.
On the Gulf, container work is overwhelmingly ILA. Breakbulk and bulk have been looser. In the 1980s, non-ILA stevedores (including at least one using Teamsters in New Orleans) competed on breakbulk, and some operators ran lower-wage “ILA lite” arrangements. The ILA’s master contract does not fully cover that cargo, so non-union or alternative-union stevedoring still exists in niches. It has not displaced ILA container gangs.
On the West Coast, the ILWU’s jurisdiction dates to the 1934 strike and the hiring-hall system that followed.

Every communist state that has ever existed faced the same fatal paradox: the party that promised to liberate the people from the oppressive state ended up building the most oppressive state in human history. This occurred not because communism attracted uniquely evil people, but because the ideology itself demanded the erasure of the line between party and state; once that line was erased, the machinery of governance became a machinery of control from which no society has ever peacefully recovered.

The deep state, a term now thrown around loosely in Western democracies to describe entrenched bureaucratic interests, was not an accident or a corruption of communism. It was communism's central organising principle. Every communist regime, from Moscow to Havana to Pyongyang, deliberately and systematically fused the party with every institution of the state until the two became indistinguishable. Understanding how they did it, and why it destroyed them, is not an exercise in Cold War nostalgia. It is a warning to every country where a ruling party with an overwhelming mandate begins to treat the state as its private property.

The Soviet Union under Lenin and Stalin created the template that every subsequent communist state would follow. The process was methodical and proceeded in identifiable stages.

First, the party captured the security apparatus. The Cheka, later the OGPU, the NKVD, and finally the KGB, was not a state institution that served the republic. It was a party organ that served the Politburo. Its officers were selected not for professional competence, but for ideological loyalty. Its mandate was not to protect citizens from crime, but to protect the party from dissent. By 1934, the NKVD had become so powerful that it operated its own economy, running the Gulag system of forced labour camps that at its peak held over 1.5 million prisoners who produced timber, mined gold, and built canals with slave labour. The security service was not merely a department of the state. It was a state within a state, answering to no court, bound by no law, and accountable to no institution except the party leadership.

Second, the party captured the judiciary. Soviet courts did not administer justice; they administered policy. Judges were party members who received instructions, sometimes explicit, sometimes implicit, on the outcomes expected in politically sensitive cases. The concept of judicial independence did not exist. Andrey Vyshinsky, Stalin's chief prosecutor during the Great Purge, openly theorised that a confession was the "queen of evidence", and confessions were extracted through torture, sleep deprivation, and threats to family members. Between 1936 and 1938, the Soviet judiciary sentenced approximately 750,000 people to death, not through any process recognisable as law, but through show trials designed to demonstrate the party's absolute power over the lives of citizens. The courts were not captured gradually. They were designed from the beginning to serve the party. There was no independent judiciary to capture because the party never permitted one to exist.

Third, the party captured the economy. The Soviet command economy eliminated private enterprise, collectivised agriculture, and placed every factory, farm, mine, and shop under state, meaning party, control. The State Planning Committee (Gosplan) set production targets for the entire economy. Factory managers were party appointees who answered to party officials, not to markets, consumers, or shareholders. The result was an economy that could build nuclear weapons and launch satellites, but could not reliably produce bread, shoes, or toilet paper. By the 1980s, the Soviet economy was spending an estimated 15 to 17 per cent of GDP on defence while its citizens queued for basic consumer goods. The economy served the party's strategic objectives, including military power, ideological prestige, and geopolitical competition, rather than the material welfare of the people it claimed to represent.

Fourth, the party captured information. Pravda, the party newspaper whose name ironically means "Truth", was the instrument through which the party controlled what citizens knew about their own country and the world. Television, radio, publishing, and education were all party-controlled. The information ecosystem was not merely censored; it was manufactured. History was rewritten to serve current political needs. Photographs were altered to remove purged officials. Statistics were fabricated to demonstrate economic progress that did not exist. When the Chernobyl nuclear reactor exploded in April 1986, the Soviet state initially denied the disaster, delayed evacuations, and suppressed information about radiation levels because the party's image mattered more than the lives of citizens living in the fallout zone. The deep state did not merely hide the truth. It replaced the truth with a party-approved alternative reality and punished anyone who pointed out the difference.

The Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, not because it was invaded, and not because its military was defeated, but because the deep state it had built over seven decades had consumed the actual state. The institutions that should have sustained the country, such as the economy, the judiciary, the civil service, and the information systems, had been so thoroughly hollowed out by party capture that when the party lost legitimacy, there was nothing left to hold the country together. The state had been replaced by the party, and when the party fell, the state fell with it.

China under Mao Zedong followed the Soviet blueprint with Chinese characteristics, and with even more devastating consequences. The Great Leap Forward (1958–1962), in which the party ordered the collectivisation of agriculture and the rapid industrialisation of rural China, resulted in the deadliest famine in human history. Estimates range from 15 million to 55 million deaths. The famine was not caused by drought or natural disaster. It was caused by the deep state: by party officials at every level who fabricated grain production figures to please their superiors, who seized food from starving villages to meet impossible quotas, and who punished anyone who reported the truth. When Peng Dehuai, a senior military commander, privately told Mao that the Great Leap Forward was failing, he was purged, imprisoned, and tortured to death during the Cultural Revolution. The system did not merely fail to prevent the famine; the system caused the famine. The fusion of party and state meant that no institution existed to challenge the party's decisions, report accurate information, or protect citizens from the consequences of ideological insanity.

The Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) was the deep state turning on itself. Mao, fearing that the party bureaucracy had become too comfortable and too independent, unleashed the Red Guards, millions of radicalised young people, to attack the very institutions the party had built. Universities were closed. Teachers were beaten, humiliated, and killed. Scientists were sent to labour in rice paddies. Cultural artefacts were destroyed. Party officials who had served the revolution for decades were dragged through the streets, forced to wear dunce caps, and publicly denounced. An estimated 1.5 to 2 million people were killed. The Cultural Revolution demonstrated the ultimate danger of the deep state: when the party is the state, and the party leader decides the state itself is the enemy, there is no institution left to restrain the destruction.

China survived where the Soviet Union did not, but only by making a calculation that would have horrified Marx: it opened the economy to capitalism while keeping the party's monopoly on political power. Deng Xiaoping's reforms after 1978 created a hybrid system, specifically a market economy generating wealth, supervised by a one-party state that retained absolute control over the judiciary, the military, the media, and the security apparatus. China's economic miracle is real, but the deep state remains. The party controls the courts; there is no independent judiciary. The party controls the internet; the Great Firewall blocks information the party considers threatening. The party controls the military; the People's Liberation Army swears allegiance to the party, not to the state or the constitution. And when the party decides that an entire ethnic group poses a threat, the deep state delivers the machinery to intern over a million Uyghurs in camps in Xinjiang with no judicial oversight, no legal process, and no accountability. China's deep state did not disappear with economic reform. It adapted, and its capacity for control is now enhanced by surveillance technology that Stalin could not have imagined.

Cuba under Fidel Castro created a deep state so total that the country has been functionally frozen since 1959. The party controls every institution: the military, the judiciary, the media, the economy, the education system, and the security apparatus. The Committees for the Defence of the Revolution (CDRs), neighbourhood surveillance organisations established on every block of every city and town, ensured that the party's eyes and ears extended into every household. Citizens who expressed dissent were reported by their neighbours, investigated by state security, and imprisoned or exiled.

The result is a country that, despite having one of the highest literacy rates and best doctor-to-patient ratios in the developing world, cannot feed its population, provide basic consumer goods, maintain its infrastructure, or offer its young people any future other than emigration. Cuba's deep state did not fail through a dramatic collapse like that of the Soviet Union. It failed through stagnation: the slow, grinding degradation of a society in which no institution exists to challenge failed policies, no court exists to protect individual rights, and no mechanism exists for peaceful political change. Cuba's buildings are crumbling. Its cars are from the 1950s. Its economy runs on remittances from the diaspora that fled the revolution. The deep state preserved the party, but it destroyed the country the party claimed to serve.

The German Democratic Republic perfected the surveillance dimension of the communist deep state. The Stasi, the Ministry for State Security, employed approximately 91,000 full-time staff and maintained a network of an estimated 189,000 civilian informants in a country of only 16 million people. That means approximately one in every 63 East Germans was reporting on their neighbours, colleagues, friends, and family members to the state security apparatus.

The Stasi did not merely monitor dissidents; it monitored everyone. It opened mail. It tapped telephones. It bugged apartments. It infiltrated churches, universities, sports clubs, and cultural organisations. It developed a practice called Zersetzung ("decomposition"), in which it systematically destroyed the personal lives of targeted individuals through rumour campaigns, career sabotage, disruption of relationships, and psychological harassment, all without the target understanding that the state was responsible. The purpose was not to imprison dissidents; that was too visible. The purpose was to break them invisibly, from the inside.

When the Berlin Wall fell in November 1989, East Germans who accessed their Stasi files discovered that their spouses, their closest friends, and even their own children had been informing on them for years. The deep state had not merely surveilled the population; it had weaponised human relationships themselves, turning trust into a tool of state control. The psychological damage persists to this day, more than 35 years later. Former East Germans report lasting difficulties with trust, intimacy, and social cohesion, which represents the intergenerational trauma of a society in which the party made every human relationship a potential instrument of betrayal.

North Korea represents the final evolution of the communist deep state: a system so total that the distinction between party, state, and reality itself has been abolished. The Kim dynasty, Kim Il-sung, Kim Jong-il, and Kim Jong-un, has achieved what no other communist regime fully accomplished: the complete replacement of objective reality with a party-constructed reality.

North Koreans do not merely live under censorship. They live inside a manufactured universe in which the Kim family possesses supernatural qualities, in which North Korea is the most prosperous and powerful nation on earth, and in which the outside world is a hellscape of poverty, exploitation, and moral degeneracy. The state controls every source of information: there is no internet, no foreign media, no independent publishing, and no uncensored communication with the outside world. Citizens who are discovered consuming foreign media, even South Korean television dramas, face imprisonment in political prison camps, where an estimated 80,000 to 120,000 people are held in conditions the United Nations has compared to Nazi concentration camps.

The deep state in North Korea does not serve any ideology, not even communism, which the regime effectively abandoned decades ago in favour of Juche (self-reliance) and Songun (military-first) doctrines. It serves only the perpetuation of the Kim family's rule. The military consumes an estimated 15 to 24 per cent of GDP while periodic famines kill tens of thousands. The party maintains control through a classification system called Songbun that assigns every citizen to one of three loyalty categories (core, wavering, or hostile) based on the political history of their ancestors. Your grandfather's political reliability in the 1950s determines your access to food, education, housing, and employment today. The deep state does not merely control the present. It has retroactively colonised the past, making every family's history a permanent political verdict from which there is no appeal.

The Khmer Rouge under Pol Pot demonstrated the most extreme consequence of the communist deep state: the point at which the party's capture of the state becomes indistinguishable from the extermination of the population. Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge emptied Cambodia's cities, abolished money, closed schools and hospitals, destroyed temples, executed intellectuals, and attempted to create an agrarian utopia through forced labour. An estimated 1.5 to 2 million people, approximately 25 per cent of Cambodia's population, died from execution, starvation, disease, and forced labour.

The deep state under the Khmer Rouge was not bureaucratic. It was eliminationist. The party decided that the existing state, society, and population were all contaminated by capitalism, imperialism, and bourgeois values, and therefore all had to be destroyed and rebuilt from zero. The security apparatus, centred on the S-21 interrogation centre at Tuol Sleng, tortured and executed approximately 17,000 people, including many of the party's own cadres, in a spiralling paranoia of purges that consumed the revolution from within. The deep state's final act was to devour itself, executing its own members on suspicion of disloyalty until the party that had destroyed a quarter of its nation's population began destroying its own leadership.

Every communist deep state, including the Soviet, Chinese, Cuban, East German, North Korean, and Cambodian regimes, followed the same structural logic.

The party captures the security services so that the instruments of force serve the party rather than the law. The party captures the judiciary so that courts deliver political outcomes rather than justice. The party captures the economy so that citizens depend on the party for their livelihoods and cannot build independent economic power. The party captures information so that citizens cannot access the facts they need to evaluate the party's performance. The party captures education so that the next generation is socialised into loyalty rather than critical thinking. And the party captures human relationships themselves, through neighbourhood committees, informant networks, and the weaponisation of trust, so that citizens cannot organise, confide, or build the social solidarity that collective action requires.

The result, in every case, is the same: a state that serves the party rather than the people; an economy that produces what the party wants rather than what the people need; a judiciary that punishes the party's enemies rather than protecting the people's rights; a security apparatus that monitors the people rather than defending them; and an information environment in which the party's version of reality replaces actual reality, until the gap between the two becomes so vast that the system collapses under the weight of its own lies.

Sri Lanka is not a communist country. The NPP/JVP government does not propose to abolish private enterprise, collectivise agriculture, or establish a one-party state. But the JVP's roots are Marxist-Leninist. Its founder, Rohana Wijeweera, was trained in Moscow. Its two insurrections, in 1971 and 1987–1989, attempted to seize the state by force. And the organisational instincts of the party, namely the discipline, the hierarchy, the suspicion of dissent, the conflation of party interests with national interests, and the treatment of critics as enemies rather than citizens, carry the DNA of the movements that built the deep states described above.

When the CIABOC Director General is identified as a former JVP legal division member, that is not a neutral staffing decision. It is the party placing its people inside the state's anti-corruption machinery. When four Supreme Court vacancies are left unfilled while sitting judges' tenures are extended by government legislation, that is the party shaping the judiciary to its advantage. When the CID questions journalists about their tweets, contacts social media platforms to demand content removal, and intelligence officers threaten citizens who participate in UN reviews, that is the party using the state's security apparatus to monitor and silence critics. When pro-government thugs break up an independent farmers' conference, that is the party using extra-state violence to suppress organizing that the party cannot control. When the Agriculture Minister calls protesting farmers "kasippu drinkers," that is the party demonstrating contempt for citizens who challenge its authority.

None of these individual acts constitutes a communist deep state. But taken together, they describe a trajectory: the gradual, incremental fusion of party and state that every communist regime began with before it metastasised into something far worse. The Soviet Union did not start with the Gulag. It started with staffing decisions, loyalty tests, the placement of party members in key institutional positions, the harassment of critics, and the conflation of dissent and treason. The Gulag came later, after the institutions that could have prevented it had already been captured.

The people of Sri Lanka do not need to wait for the Gulag to recognise the pattern. They need to recognise it now: while the institutions that protect them still exist, while the judiciary still has some independence, while the media can still report, while citizens can still organise, while elections still happen, and while the line between government and state has been blurred but not yet erased. Because every country that waited until the line was fully erased discovered the same truth: by then, there was nothing left to fight with, no institution left to appeal to, and no mechanism left for peaceful change. The deep state had consumed the state. And the people, the people in whose name the revolution was always conducted, had nothing left but the party's version of reality and the party's definition of freedom.

That is the lesson of every communist deep state: not that communism attracts bad people, but that the fusion of party and state, regardless of the intentions behind it, inevitably produces a system that serves the party at the expense of the people. Sri Lanka must decide now, not later, whether it will permit that fusion to continue or whether it will defend the independence of the institutions that belong to its citizens, not to any party. The answer to that question will determine whether Sri Lanka remains a democracy with problems or becomes another cautionary tale in the long, bloody history of states that were consumed by the parties that claimed to serve them.

A war-band can take a peninsula and still not own its own story. Muhammad died in Medina in June 632. Within a generation his men were not reciting one fixed text. According to the Sunni canon itself—Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 and 5102—Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, campaigning in Armenia and Azerbaijan under the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan (r. 644–656), heard Syrian and Iraqi soldiers accusing one another over variant readings of the Qur’an and feared schism. Uthman ordered Zayd ibn Thabit and a small committee to produce one official recension from the sheets already gathered under Abu Bakr after the battle of Yamamah (c. 632–633), sent copies to the main garrison cities, and commanded that other written collections be burned. That is not how a father handles truth. That is how a commander handles a riot in camp. The man of the raid had offered fighting men what fighting men already priced—women, spoil, rank, a paradise with the smell of victory on it—and he got his army: Hijrah 622, Badr 624, the taking of Mecca in 630, a community armed enough that, after 632, it walked out of Arabia and broke the near frontiers of Byzantium and Ctesiphon. He did not get control of the wording. The sword can gather a host. It cannot keep ten mouths from rewriting the banner. When the banner starts a fight, the caliph does not repent. He lights a fire under the other pages (Bukhari 4987).

That is the method. Feed the pack. Win the ground. When the story cracks, burn the variants. A hunter plates the hunger. He does not remake it.

Now the other table.

The gospel is still the worst product in the shop. No one designing customers writes it. Someone who wants sons writes it. Soft men swollen with appetite will always walk to the louder stall. That walk is not evidence. It is the x-ray. And it leaves Jesus where He stands: above the stall, the legion, and every cheap replacement—worthy, because He refused to purchase us with our vice. He paid in blood.

God is not recruiting buyers. He is calling children home.

Jesus does not bait Jew or Greek with their favorite dish. He orders both to drop the plate.

The Jew wanted a war-crown: Rome thrown off, Zion armed, a Messiah who wins like Caesar. Jesus answers with timber and nails, under Pontius Pilate, c. 30–33. “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). Come back to the Father. Receive a name. “To all who received Him, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

The Gentile wanted the old night: the body as shrine, the feast that never closes, the rot Paul names in the streets around the churches (Romans 1; 1 Corinthians 5–6). Jesus answers with a cut. Stop staring. Tear out the eye (Matthew 5:27–32). One covenant bed. Rule the flesh. Then live as a son, not as a stomach.

He does not toss steak to the wolf. He puts bread in a mouth that only knew raw meat—and then dies and rises so the mouth can say Abba. No harem as wages. Adoption. The Lamb dies for the enemy. The stone rolls.

Muhammad runs the opposite shop. He wanted a host and he bought one with the inventory the host already priced: raids for caravan wealth after 622, plural marriage written into law, captives as a lawful yield of war. That raises banners. It does not raise sons of God. And when the inventory of words would not sit still, Uthman, about 650–653, burned the extras. Army first. Canon by bonfire second.

Look at what grows, without perfume. Where Christ’s gospel actually entered—not the costume of Christ, the command of Christ—even under crooked kings, a strange orchard appeared: the weak life counts, the child is not a clan chip only, the woman is not a share of loot, letters and universities sprout because a soul is addressed by God and must learn to answer. Cathedral schools and the medieval universitas—Bologna (1088), Paris (c. 1150), Oxford (c. 1096)—did not grow from a tent of captives. They grew from a Cross and from “let the little children come to Me” (Mark 10:14).

A creed built to please the raider will not pause and see woman and child as the image of God. It will see them as cargo—flesh, hush, wall. Useful falsehood, sanctified war, the killing of the holdout, poverty called fate: that is not bad weather on the map. That is what you plant when desire wears a scabbard.

If truth were the average male wish, heaven would be unemployed. We already know the wish: more body, more force, more alibi. That wish is the clay of this century—in the old paganism that still rides under a prophet’s name, and in the new ideologies that spit on the church. Both want a homemade god. One names it caliphate. One names it State. Both say the vote of man is the verdict of right. That sentence is not faith. It is apostasy with a flag.

The hunter blesses the pulse. The Father breaks it and names it child. That is why the gospel still will not sell to synagogue or forum. And that is why Jesus still has no rival: He would rather lose the crowd than nurse the fever. He lost the crowd. He kept the empty tomb. He kept the way back to the Father.

🇵🇰 A CLEAR MESSAGE FROM RAWALPINDI: ASIM MUNIR LAYS OUT PAKISTAN’S SECURITY PRIORITIES

From Terrorism and Border Security to Internal Stability, Saudi Arabia and Modern Warfare — The Army Chief’s Latest Message

Pakistan’s top military leadership has delivered a wide-ranging security message amid a rapidly changing regional environment.

On October 2, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff, chaired the 277th Corps Commanders’ Conference at General Headquarters in Rawalpindi.

The meeting reviewed Pakistan’s internal and external security environment and reaffirmed the armed forces’ readiness to respond to emerging threats.

🛡️ A FIRM WARNING ON INTERNAL INSTABILITY

One of the strongest messages emerging from the meeting concerned internal stability.

The military leadership said that any attempt to create unrest resembling the May 9, 2023 disturbances would be met with decisive action under the rule of law.

The statement specifically stressed that such action would be taken without hesitation or discrimination.

The message comes ahead of a planned political march toward Islamabad and amid heightened political tensions in the country.

🇵🇰 PAKISTAN’S RIGHT TO SELF-DEFENCE

The conference also focused heavily on terrorism originating from Afghanistan.

The commanders reaffirmed Pakistan’s position that the country has the right to defend itself against cross-border terrorism and emphasized the need for targeted action against terrorist threats.

The military statement placed responsibility for consequences on the Taliban leadership over what Pakistan describes as facilitation of terrorism.

At the same time, the leadership discussed combining security operations with political, administrative and community-level measures.

🎯 A TWO-SIDED APPROACH TO COUNTER-TERRORISM

The military leadership did not frame the response solely around kinetic operations.

The conference highlighted a broader strategy involving:

• Intelligence-based operations
• Stronger policing capacity
• Grassroots governance
• Greater engagement with the public
• Action against the alleged terror-crime nexus
• Continued implementation of the National Action Plan
• Progress under Vision Azm-e-Istehkam

The emphasis was therefore on combining security action with measures designed to address the wider environment in which terrorism and organized crime operate.

🇸🇦🇹🇷 PAKISTAN REAFFIRMS SAUDI-TÜRKİYE DEFENCE COOPERATION

Another major element of the meeting was Pakistan’s recently established defence relationship with Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.

The commanders welcomed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, describing it as an important development in the three countries’ long-standing strategic and collective-defence ties.

The forum also condemned Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and reiterated Pakistan’s commitment to the security and sanctity of Haramain Sharifain.

This comes as regional security dynamics remain highly sensitive.

🇮🇳 KASHMIR REMAINS ON THE MILITARY AGENDA

The conference also reiterated Pakistan’s established position regarding Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir.

According to the ISPR statement, the military leadership again called for resolution of the Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of Kashmiris.

⚔️ MODERN WARFARE AND NEW TECHNOLOGY

Field Marshal Asim Munir also placed emphasis on the future battlefield.

He directed commanders to continue improving:

Intelligence capabilities

Operational preparedness

Combat effectiveness

Modern technology integration

Training

Multi-domain military coordination

The direction reflects the increasing importance of technology, intelligence and integrated capabilities in modern warfare.

🫡 TRIBUTE TO THOSE WHO LOST THEIR LIVES

The conference also offered prayers for members of the armed forces, law-enforcement agencies and civilians who lost their lives in service of Pakistan.
